related_resources.reason: Scholarly contemporary account by a fellow physicist: family, Pisa/European training, Rome group, neutron work, limitations of uranium interpretation, migration, Columbia, first pile, Hanford, Los Alamos, and late research. Recollections are retrospective.
Overview, dates, family and career, archive scope; not a claim that individual archival letters or notebooks were all inspected.
Archival exhibit on family photographs, field visits and teaching through Rome, New York and Chicago.
1938 racial laws and departure after Nobel awards.
Laura Capon Fermi as author and civic figure; Atoms in the Family (1954); papers are mainly her own writing, not direct evidence for every event in Enrico’s career.
Laura’s 1954 memoir as authored account with its own perspective.
Schooling, brother Giulio, early friendship and quantum statistics; retrospective biographical material.
Detailed Italian-language scholarly account, including Giulio, early friendship and Roman institutions.
Primary account of 1934 induced radioactivity, neutron method and attribution to the Joliot-Curies. Historical interpretations in the lecture are those of 1938.
Contemporaneous prize language claims new elements and credits slow-neutron reactions; reflects pre-fission identification, not proof that transuranics were found in 1934.
Via Panisperna experimental sequence and purpose of neutron-induced experiments; first-person narration is museum presentation, not a historical first-person transcript.
Fermi and Dirac’s 1926 developments and priority correspondence; simplified museum pedagogical language distinguished from literal physics.
Archival and historiographic context for the 1926 independent research and theoretical distinctions.
General history and Fermi–Dirac explanation, beta decay, and experimental career; supplementary.
Contemporaneous account of beta spectrum problem and experimental evidence for antineutrino; not retrospective proof that Fermi observed one.
1934 transuranic interpretation, subsequent work by Meitner, Hahn, Strassmann and Frisch; evaluates priority under persecution and exile.
Career chronology, New York/Chicago/Los Alamos, citizenship, Nobel and scientific contributions. Broad summary, subordinate to precise archival dates.
December 2 1942 setting, George Weil, others present, duration and Wigner’s Chianti.
Leona Woods’s neutron counting work and membership in Chicago pile team.
Independent team identification and detector work, with some contemporaneous detail of credential dates differing across short biographies.
Hanford reactor startup, 1944 work, Chicago/Los Alamos chronology; crosscheck NAS memoir for xenon details.
Direct primary document for the paper-drop and its approximately ten-kiloton estimate.
Modern technical reconstruction of paper experiment, limited historical account of exactly how Fermi computed the result.
Signed Fermi–Rabi position against pursuing the thermonuclear super; not a measure of earlier atomic bomb views.
1953 nonlinear computation, title-page/footnote credit and Mary Tsingou’s coding; retrospective historical framing.
Original report deposited in digital repository, begun before Fermi death and completed after it; author credits vary by catalog versus title-page layout.
Direct excerpt of numerical results, nonlinear recurrence and dates; present-day authorship discussion.
1980s correspondence and participant recollections; exact wording and date uncertain, apparently about summer 1950.
Professional life, war, 1938 flight, Chicago, and postwar career.

description: Traces Enrico Fermi from quantum statistics and his theory of beta decay through neutron experiments and the first controlled nuclear chain reaction. Connects his theoretical and experimental methods to scientific migration, collaborative research, cosmic-ray acceleration and numerical experiments on nonlinear dynamics.
